title: Why Is This So Hard? On Workload, Pressure, and the Ways through the Woods
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Eleven days into the 2020-2021 school year, Dave Stuart Jr. names the question he and countless colleagues were quietly asking themselves: why does this year feel so much harder than any prior year, including his own first years of teaching? He diagnoses the difficulty as a 'vicious partnership' between rapidly increased workload (more emails, more troubleshooting, more students to accommodate across in-person, quarantined, and virtual configurations at once) and rapidly increased pressure (political, financial, emotional, social), each of which feeds the other in a reinforcing loop. Drawing on the Yerkes-Dodson Law, he explains that pressure past a certain point degrades thinking and performance, which increases workload, which increases pressure further. His proposed way through the woods has three parts: reset internal expectations and measuring sticks rather than judging the year by normal-year standards, invest in deeper and more disciplined self-care across physical, emotional, social, and spiritual dimensions, and attack the workload itself through disciplined learning, thinking, collaborating, and execution. The piece is explicitly framed as an attempt at hope rather than mere commiseration, closing with concrete 'good enough' benchmarks to replace pre-pandemic standards of excellence.
points: The year's difficulty stems from a 'vicious partnership' between rapidly rising workload and rapidly rising pressure, each of which reinforces and amplifies the other via the Yerkes-Dodson relationship between pressure and performance.

Much of the added 2020 workload is uniquely hard to manage because it is not skippable, is genuinely difficult, or is too new to know how important it actually is — unlike ordinary too-much-to-do, which experienced teachers usually know how to triage.
Managing internal pressure requires deliberately resetting the 'measuring stick' used to judge the year, replacing pre-pandemic standards of excellence with explicit 'good enough' benchmarks.
Self-care during crisis needs to be a disciplined, learned practice — treating other people's coping strategies as data to collect and try, not a set of shallow 'life hack' platitudes.
quotes: I expected the year to be different — but I didn't expect to be drowning in a way that I haven't felt since my first years.
I began asking more people how they were doing. I was surprised at how few were doing well.
But the workload this year is especially hard because the added task volume is A) not skippable, B) very difficult, or C) too new to know how important it is.
Pressure makes our minds mushy. It makes giving in to distraction easier. It goads us into using brute force — working harder — to solve problems that require tactical savvy.
I'll say it: we may need to sacrifice or severely modify our pedagogy this year. I'm starting to accept this.
Times like this call for deeper, longer draws from the springs of well-being — not shallower, quicker ones.

We've got to approach this like learners. When someone you are with shares something that helps them in the physical or mental or emotional or spiritual or social elements of their lives, get out the notebook. Write it down.
